groups.text: You want to know where feeSlow spends its C P U time, without changing its code.
Here is the thread's call stack.
Thread.run is the root, at the bottom.
Each method sits on top of the one that called it.
The top frame is where the C P U is right now.
The stack changes all the time.
A sampling profiler is a loop: every ten ms, it takes a snapshot of the stack.
Then it counts identical stacks.
One line per stack, with its count: this text is what every flame graph tool reads.
To draw a flame graph, the tool first sorts the stacks alphabetically, by full class name.
Not by time: the sample from twenty ms ends up on the right.
Then identical frames at the same depth, under the same parent, merge into one box.
When each sample was taken is gone.
So each box is one frame, and its width is the number of samples with that frame on the stack.
String.format was on four of the nine.
feeSlow was on all nine, so it spans the whole width.
And left to right is the alphabet, not a timeline.
flamegraph.pl's own header says it: the ordering on the x-axis has no meaning.
Now look at the tops.
The part of a box with nothing above it is self time: the C P U was in that frame's own code.
Wide tops are where to start.
feeSlow is wide, but covered by its children.
It does little itself and calls expensive things, so the fix is usually in one of them.
This is feeSlow in a real C P U profile of the same fee code, zoomed in.
It covered five thousand seven hundred forty-seven of eight thousand five samples: seventy-one point eight%.
Walk up from that wide plateau.
Its widest children are String.format, with twenty-three point three% of all samples, and Pattern.compile, with seventeen point six%.
Then toPlainString, with eleven point five%, and the BigDecimal constructor, with seven point nine%.
Pattern.compile builds a regex on every call.
Move it into a static final field, and that whole tower, about eighteen percent of the samples, goes away.
Width is samples.
Left to right is the alphabet.
And the tops are where the C P U was.
